questions.question: What is a Large Language Model (LLM)?
options: A rule-based system that matches keywords to predefined responses
A neural network trained on large amounts of text data to understand and generate language
A database that stores and retrieves pre-written sentences
A computer program that translates between programming languages
questions.explanation: An LLM is a deep neural network—typically based on the transformer architecture—trained on massive text corpora to learn statistical patterns of language, enabling it to understand and generate human-like text.

questions.question: What does 'tokenisation' mean in the context of LLMs?
options: Encrypting text data before feeding it to a model
Breaking raw text into smaller units (tokens) that the model processes
Converting model weights into binary format for storage
Splitting a dataset into training and test sets
questions.explanation: Tokenisation converts raw text into a sequence of tokens—which can be words, subwords, or characters—that the model can process numerically. Models like GPT use Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) to create subword tokens.

questions.question: In LLMs, what does the 'temperature' parameter control?
options: The speed of text generation
The maximum number of tokens the model can generate
The randomness or creativity of the model's output
The number of layers in the neural network
questions.explanation: Temperature scales the logits before applying softmax to compute token probabilities. A higher temperature (e.g., 1.5) makes the distribution flatter and outputs more random, while a lower temperature (e.g., 0.1) makes it sharper and more deterministic.

questions.question: What is the 'context window' of an LLM?
options: The graphical interface used to interact with the model
The maximum number of tokens the model can consider at one time
The set of training examples used to fine-tune the model
The memory allocated on the GPU during inference
questions.explanation: The context window is the maximum number of tokens (input + output) an LLM can process in a single forward pass. Tokens outside this window are not visible to the model.

questions.question: BERT is a decoder-only transformer model, similar in architecture to GPT.
questions.explanation: BERT is an encoder-only model that uses bidirectional attention to read the full input context simultaneously. GPT is decoder-only and uses causal (left-to-right) attention. BERT is better for understanding tasks; GPT for generation.

questions.question: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?
options: A technique to train LLMs faster using less data
A method that combines a retrieval system with an LLM to ground responses in external documents
A way to compress model weights for faster inference
A reinforcement learning approach to improve model alignment
questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant documents from an external knowledge base at inference time and provides them as context to the LLM, allowing the model to produce responses grounded in up-to-date or domain-specific information without retraining.

questions.question: In zero-shot prompting, you provide the model with several labelled examples before asking it to answer a question.
questions.explanation: Zero-shot prompting gives the model no examples—it relies entirely on its pre-trained knowledge. Few-shot prompting is the technique that provides labelled examples (shots) in the prompt to guide the model's behaviour.

questions.question: The transformer architecture relies on a mechanism called ______ to weigh the importance of different tokens relative to one another.
questions.explanation: The attention mechanism computes a weighted sum of value vectors based on query-key similarity, allowing each token to directly attend to every other token in the sequence regardless of distance.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes 'embeddings' in the context of LLMs?
options: Binary flags that indicate whether a token is a noun or verb
Dense numerical vector representations of tokens or text that capture semantic meaning
The model's output probabilities over its entire vocabulary
Compressed versions of model weights stored on disk
questions.explanation: Embeddings are dense, continuous vector representations learned during training. Semantically similar words or phrases end up with similar vectors, enabling reasoning about meaning and powering vector databases.

questions.question: LLMs can hallucinate—generating text that sounds plausible but is factually incorrect.
questions.explanation: Hallucination occurs because LLMs generate tokens based on statistical patterns rather than by looking up verified facts. They can confidently produce incorrect names, dates, citations, or events that never happened.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)?
options: To increase the size of a model's vocabulary
To align model outputs with human preferences by training on human-ranked responses
To reduce the model's memory footprint for edge deployment
To speed up tokenisation during inference
questions.explanation: RLHF fine-tunes a pre-trained LLM using a reward model trained on human preference data. The language model is then optimised with reinforcement learning (typically PPO) to generate responses that score highly according to the reward model.

questions.question: GPT models use a ______-only transformer architecture, processing tokens left to right.
questions.explanation: GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) is a decoder-only model that uses causal (unidirectional) self-attention, allowing each token to attend only to preceding tokens. This makes it naturally suited for autoregressive text generation.

questions.question: What does 'top-p sampling' (nucleus sampling) do when generating text?
options: Always selects the single token with the highest probability
Samples from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p
Selects the top k tokens by probability and samples uniformly from them
Applies a penalty to repeated tokens to reduce repetition
questions.explanation: Top-p (nucleus) sampling builds a dynamic vocabulary of the most probable tokens until their cumulative probability reaches p (e.g., 0.9), then samples from that set. This adapts to the confidence of the model.

questions.question: Fine-tuning an LLM always requires retraining all of the model's original weights.
questions.explanation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA and adapters allow fine-tuning by updating only a small number of additional parameters while keeping the original model weights frozen, drastically reducing compute and memory requirements.

questions.question: Which architecture does the T5 model use?
options: Encoder-only, like BERT
Decoder-only, like GPT
Encoder-decoder, processing input with an encoder and generating output with a decoder
A recurrent neural network with attention gates
questions.explanation: T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer) uses a full encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder processes the input sequence, and the decoder autoregressively generates the output, making it flexible for tasks like translation and summarisation.
